topic: Why SMS two-factor codes are risky
hook: Your phone suddenly shows no signal.
visual_style: Photorealistic cinematic film still, real materials and textures, shallow depth of field, moody city night, cool blue light with warning red accents, rain reflections
world: A big American city on a rainy night today, neon reflections on wet streets
through_line: one phone's signal, lost to a stranger and then locked back down

cast.Owner: a woman in her 30s, long black hair in a low ponytail, olive green jacket
cast.Thief: a man in his 30s in a dark baseball cap and grey hoodie, face in shadow

props.Phone: a black smartphone whose screen shows only plain glowing shapes and no words
props.SIM card: a tiny SIM card with a gold chip

places.Street: a rainy city street at night, neon reflections on wet pavement
places.Back room: a dim back room with a cluttered desk and two glowing monitors

cta: Set this up tonight, and share it with someone who uses text codes.

captions.hook_line: Your 2FA text codes can be stolen without anyone touching your phone 📱
captions.body: In a SIM swap, a criminal convinces your carrier to move your number to their SIM, then receives your text-message login codes. Authenticator apps, security keys and passkeys are stronger. Move your email first, since it can reset other accounts, and ask your carrier about a port-out PIN or number lock.
captions.comment_prompt: Are you still using text codes for your email?

youtube_title: Why Text Message Codes Aren't Safe Enough

blocks.narration: Your phone suddenly shows no signal. Somewhere else, a stranger is now getting every login code you are sent.
blocks.visual: The Owner on the rainy Street staring at her Phone as its screen flashes red

shots.visual: The Owner on the rainy Street staring at her Phone as its screen flashes red
The Thief in the Back room grinning as a phone on his desk lights up with a new message

blocks.narration: It is called a SIM swap. A criminal calls your carrier pretending to be you, and moves your number to their own SIM.
blocks.visual: Tweezers sliding the SIM card into a phone tray on the Back room desk

shots.visual: Tweezers sliding the SIM card into a phone tray on the Back room desk
The Thief speaking into a phone in the Back room in a calm friendly voice, reading from his monitor
The Thief holding up a phone whose screen fills with full signal bars

blocks.narration: Now your two-factor text codes go straight to them. Your email falls first, then banking, then every social account.
blocks.visual: A phone on the Back room desk lighting up again and again with new message bubbl

shots.visual: A phone on the Back room desk lighting up again and again with new message bubbles
The Owner under a neon sign on the Street, her Phone dark, rain falling harder

blocks.narration: Authenticator apps and passkeys never travel by text. Move your email over first, because email can reset everything else.
blocks.visual: The Owner holding her Phone as a plain green shield shape glows on the screen

shots.visual: The Owner holding her Phone as a plain green shield shape glows on the screen
A thumb tapping the Phone screen, a plain envelope shape turning green

blocks.narration: Then ask your carrier for a number lock or port-out PIN. Then a dead signal never hands a stranger your codes.

The Thief's phone in the Back room going dark, his grin fading
